catalog_quote: Ende does not have lexical stress or tone. There are no words in the current lexicon that minimally contrast by something like stress, and tonelessness is a typological feature of the region (Evans et al. 2018: 738). Intonational frames are poorly understood in the language. Questions do not systemat- ically end in a rising tune and are often falling, even though word order does not always indicate whether or not the utterance is a question or a statement. One interesting use of intonation is the Call-at-Distance form. ... The Call-at-Distance form is located at the end of an utterance and entails final vowel lengthening, the addition of /-oː/ or /-aj/, and a considerable rise in pitch and loudness, especially for questions

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ende has no lexical (contrastive) word stress and no tone; the author found no minimal pairs by stress and speakers cannot reliably locate a stressed syllable. No default or phonetic stress position is described.
new_statements.exceptions: None. The dissertation notes that stress judgments by speakers 'often change from one day to the next' and that stresslessness may be an areal feature of South Fly.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexicon statement: no lexical stress, no tone, no minimal pairs by stress. Intonation is described only at utterance level (question tunes not systematic; a Call-at-Distance form with final lengthening, /-oː/ or /-aj/ suffix, and pitch/loudness rise). The 2019 dissertation (p. 158) adds that speakers cannot consistently identify stressed syllables, so no phonetic default position is reported either.
new_statements.identity_note: Both sources describe Ende (Limol village, Western Province, PNG), one variety under the Glottolog language-level node agob1244 Agob-Ende-Kawam [kit]; the Pahoturi River family also includes Agob, Em, Kawam (under this node) and Idi/Taeme (idii1243). No stress description was found for the Agob or Kawam varieties themselves; older records for Agob/Dabu/Kawam/Kibuli in Glottolog are wordlists only (Chalmers 1897/1903, Lyons 1914, Karius 1926).

sources.note: Appendix A 'Linguistic profile of Ende', §A.2.3 'The word', p. 158 (PDF p. 188): 'There is no contrastive tone in Ende, and stress does not seem to be a distinctive feature. Speakers find picking out stressed syllables difficult, and judgments often change from one day to the next. There are no words in the current lexicon that minimally contrast by something like stress. According to other researchers who work in the geographical area of South Fly, Papua New Guinea, this property of stresslessness is common and may be an areal feature.' No stress rule given anywhere else in the 384-page PDF…
